# CSR Register File Behavioral Specification

## 1. Overview

The module implements the control and status register (CSR) file for the CVA6 core. Its primary responsibilities are:

- Providing read, write, set, and clear access to the implemented RISC-V CSRs.
- Enforcing privilege-level and debug-mode access rules.
- Raising an illegal-instruction exception when a CSR access is not permitted.
- Maintaining machine, supervisor, floating-point, debug, translation, PMP, and custom control state.
- Handling trap entry, trap delegation, interrupt pending/enable state, and trap-return behavior.
- Supporting debug-mode entry, single-step behavior, and WFI halt/restart.
- Providing address-translation, cache, accelerator, and performance-counter control outputs.

All state is clocked by a single clock and reset asynchronously, active low.

---

## 2. Reset and Initialization

On reset, the module must initialize all architectural state to its reset value:

- Privilege level is machine mode.
- Debug mode is disabled.
- Address translation is disabled.
- All floating-point CSRs are zero.
- All machine and supervisor trap CSRs are zero.
- All PMP configuration and address registers are zero.
- Cycle and instruction-retired counters are zero.
- The cache-enable CSRs are reset to enabled.
- The accelerator memory-consistency control is reset to enabled if the accelerator is configured, otherwise it is unavailable.
- The debug control/status register is reset with debug version set to 4 and previous privilege set to machine mode.
- The machine trap-vector base is initialized, after reset, to the configured boot address plus an offset of `0x40`.

---

## 3. CSR Access Semantics

### 3.1 Access Operations

The module must support the standard CSR access operations:

- Read: returns the current CSR value and performs no write.
- Write: writes the supplied data to the CSR.
- Set: writes the bitwise OR of the supplied data and the current CSR value.
- Clear: writes the current CSR value with the supplied bits cleared.

### 3.2 Privilege Checking

Every CSR address encodes the minimum privilege level required to access it. The module must permit access only if the current effective privilege level is at least the required privilege level. Otherwise, the access is denied and an illegal-instruction exception is generated.

The module must also enforce the following special access rules:

- Debug-only CSRs are accessible only while the hart is in debug mode. Access from outside debug mode raises an illegal-instruction exception.
- Counter and counter-shadow CSRs are accessible from S-mode only if the corresponding bit in the machine counter-enable register is set, and from U-mode only if both the machine and supervisor counter-enable registers permit the access.
- Reads and writes to the supervisor address-translation register are illegal when executed in S-mode while the `TVM` (trap virtual memory) bit in `mstatus` is set.

### 3.3 Illegal Accesses

An illegal CSR access is one of:

- Access to a CSR that is not implemented.
- Access with insufficient privilege.
- Access to a debug-only CSR from outside debug mode.
- Write to a read-only or write-ignored CSR where the architecture requires an exception.
- Access to a counter CSR inhibited by the counter-enable mechanism.

On any illegal CSR access, the module must:

- Suppress all CSR read and write side effects.
- Report an illegal-instruction exception.
- Leave architectural state unchanged.

Read-only and WARL fields must follow their defined behavior: unsupported write values are ignored or legalized as appropriate.

---

## 4. CSR Groups and Behavior

### 4.1 Floating-Point CSRs

The floating-point CSRs are implemented only when the floating-point extension is configured.

- The accrued-exception flags register contains five exception flags: invalid operation, divide-by-zero, overflow, underflow, and inexact.
- The dynamic rounding-mode register contains the three-bit rounding mode.
- The combined floating-point control/status register packs the rounding mode and accrued exception flags.
- A custom floating-point precision-control register is also provided.

Behavior:

- Writes to floating-point CSRs must mark the floating-point extension state as dirty.
- Writes to floating-point CSRs must request a pipeline flush because they can affect subsequent floating-point behavior.
- Retiring a floating-point instruction accumulates new exception flags into the accrued-exception flags using a logical OR.
- An imprecise floating-point exception from an optional accelerator must be accumulated into the accrued-exception flags immediately when it is signalled.
- If the floating-point extension is not configured, all floating-point CSRs are treated as unimplemented: reads and writes are illegal.

### 4.2 Machine-Mode CSRs

The module must implement the machine-mode CSRs listed below.

#### `mstatus`

The machine-status register holds global interrupt enables, previous privilege/interrupt-enable state, MPRV, MXR, SUM, TVM/TW/TSR, extension state, and dirty-state summary.

- Writes to `mstatus` must update the implemented fields.
- Reserved WPRI fields are cleared.
- The SXL and UXL fields are forced to the configured `XLEN` value.
- The XS field is forced to `Off`.
- The FS and VS fields are forced to `Off` when the corresponding extension is not configured.
- The FS field must be set to `Dirty` on a write to any floating-point CSR or when a floating-point instruction retires.
- The VS field must be set to `Dirty` when vector state becomes dirty.
- The SD bit summarizes whether any implemented extension state is dirty.
- A write to `mstatus` must request a pipeline flush.

#### `misa`

The machine-ISA register must read as the configured ISA code, indicating the supported base ISA width and extensions. Writes are ignored.

#### `medeleg` and `mideleg`

These registers delegate synchronous exceptions and interrupts to S-mode.

- `medeleg` must provide writable bits for the implemented synchronous exceptions: instruction address misaligned, breakpoint, environment call from U-mode, instruction page fault, load page fault, and store page fault. All other bits read as zero.
- `mideleg` must provide writable bits for supervisor software interrupt, supervisor timer interrupt, and supervisor external interrupt. All other bits read as zero.

#### `mie` and `mip`

The machine interrupt-enable and interrupt-pending registers.

- `mie` must implement the machine and supervisor software, timer, and external interrupt enable bits. Writes to unsupported bits are ignored.
- `mip` must reflect:
  - Machine external interrupt pending from the external interrupt input.
  - Machine software interrupt pending from the inter-processor interrupt input.
  - Machine timer interrupt pending from the timer interrupt input.
  - Supervisor software, timer, and external pending bits, with the software-writable supervisor bits writable as defined.
- Reads of `mip` must combine the software-writable supervisor external pending bit with the supervisor external interrupt input.
- Reads of `sip` must similarly combine the delegated supervisor external pending bit with the supervisor external interrupt input.

#### `mtvec`

The machine trap-vector base register.

- Supports direct and vectored modes.
- The mode is selected by the least-significant bit.
- In direct mode, the vector base is 4-byte aligned.
- In vectored mode, the implementation enforces the additional alignment required by the vectored mode.

#### `mcounteren` and `mcountinhibit`

- `mcounteren` controls S-mode and U-mode access to the counter CSRs.
- `mcountinhibit` controls whether the cycle counter, instruction-retired counter, and hardware performance counters increment.
- Bit 0 inhibits the cycle counter.
- Bit 2 inhibits the instruction-retired counter.
- Higher implemented bits inhibit the corresponding hardware performance counters.

#### `mscratch`, `mepc`, `mcause`, `mtval`

- `mscratch` is a general-purpose machine scratch register.
- `mepc` holds the machine exception program counter. Writes clear the least-significant bit.
- `mcause` holds the machine trap cause.
- `mtval` holds the machine trap value.

#### Machine ID Registers

The module must provide read-only access to:

- Machine vendor ID.
- Machine architecture ID.
- Machine implementation ID.
- Machine hardware thread ID from the hart ID input.
- Machine configuration pointer. This register is read-only; when no configuration data structure is provided, permitted reads return zero without raising an illegal-instruction exception.

#### `mstatush`

On RV32, this register reads as zero and writes are ignored. On RV64, accesses to this register are illegal.

### 4.3 Supervisor-Mode CSRs

#### `sstatus`

The supervisor-status register is a subset of `mstatus`.

- It exposes the implemented supervisor-visible status bits.
- Writes modify only the fields defined in `sstatus`.
- Writes to `sstatus` must request a pipeline flush.
- If floating-point or vector extensions are not configured, the corresponding state fields are forced to `Off`.

#### `sie` and `sip`

Supervisor interrupt-enable and interrupt-pending CSRs.

- Reads of `sie` return the machine interrupt-enable bits masked by the interrupt-delegation register.
- Writes to `sie` update only the bits delegated to S-mode.
- Reads of `sip` return the machine interrupt-pending bits masked by the interrupt-delegation register.
- Writes to `sip` update only the writable supervisor software-pending bit when it is delegated.

#### `stvec`

The supervisor trap-vector base register.

- Supports direct and vectored modes.
- Writes force the vector-base alignment required by the implemented modes.

#### `scounteren`

The supervisor counter-enable register controls U-mode access to counter CSRs.

#### `sscratch`, `sepc`, `scause`, `stval`

- `sscratch` is a supervisor scratch register.
- `sepc` holds the supervisor exception program counter. Writes clear the least-significant bit.
- `scause` holds the supervisor trap cause.
- `stval` holds the supervisor trap value.

#### `satp`

The supervisor address-translation register.

- Reads and writes are permitted in S-mode and M-mode, except that S-mode accesses are illegal when `TVM` is set.
- The mode field supports Bare mode and the configured page-based mode.
- Writes selecting an unsupported mode are ignored.
- The ASID field is masked to the configured number of implemented ASID bits.
- A write to `satp` must request a pipeline flush.

### 4.4 Debug and Trigger CSRs

Debug CSRs are accessible only from debug mode.

#### `dcsr`

The debug control/status register.

- Debug version is fixed to 4.
- The non-maskable interrupt pending bit is read-only zero.
- The stop-count and stop-time bits are read-only zero.
- The previous-privilege field records the privilege level at debug entry.
- The cause field records why debug mode was entered.
- The step, stepie, mprven, and ebreak enable bits control debug behavior.

#### `dpc`

Holds the debug PC. When debug mode is entered, it is updated to the appropriate resume address. Software in debug mode may write it to change the resume address.

#### `dscratch0` and `dscratch1`

General-purpose debug scratch registers.

#### Trigger CSRs

The trigger module CSRs are not implemented. They must read as zero and writes must be ignored.

### 4.5 Custom Cache and Accelerator CSRs

The module implements custom control registers for:

- Instruction cache enable.
- Data cache enable.
- Accelerator memory-consistency mode.

Each of these registers stores a single enable bit in the least-significant position; writes to upper bits are ignored.

- The data cache enable output follows the data cache control register.
- The instruction cache enable output follows the instruction cache control register, and in the standard configuration is suppressed while in debug mode.
- The accelerator memory-consistency output is active only when the accelerator is configured; otherwise the CSR is inaccessible and the output is disabled.

### 4.6 Physical Memory Protection (PMP)

The module implements up to 16 PMP entries, with the implemented number of entries configurable.

- PMP configuration is stored in byte-wide per-entry configuration registers, grouped into configuration CSRs.
- PMP address registers store the physical-address upper bits for each entry.
- Entries beyond the configured count are forced to zero and writes are ignored.

PMP behavior:

- PMP address granularity is 8 bytes.
- The `NA4` mode is not supported.
- Illegal encoding with read=0 and write=1 is not supported.
- Writes selecting an unsupported mode must be ignored.
- A locked PMP entry cannot be modified.
- The address register immediately below a locked TOR entry also cannot be modified.
- Reads of PMP address registers reflect the appropriate WARL behavior for the configured address mode: for NAPOT mode, the low bit reads as 1; for TOR/OFF modes, the low bit reads as 0.

### 4.7 Counters and Performance Monitoring

The module implements:

- `mcycle` and its upper half.
- `minstret` and its upper half.
- Read-only user-mode shadows of the cycle capabilitiy and instruction-retired counters.
- Access to configurable hardware performance-monitoring event selectors and counters through an external performance-counter interface.

Behavior:

- The cycle counter increments each cycle unless inhibited, unless the hart is in debug mode.
- The instruction-retired counter increments by the number of instructions retired in a cycle, unless inhibited, unless an exception is taken in the same cycle, or unless the hart is in debug mode.
- Writes to the lower and upper halves of the machine counters are supported.
- Upper-half counter accesses are legal only on RV32. On RV64, upper-half counter CSR accesses are illegal.
- Event selector and hardware performance-counter accesses are forwarded to the external performance-counter unit.
- The external unit supplies read data; the module supplies the address, write data, and write-enable for the access.
- Unavailable performance counters and event selectors read as zero and writes are ignored.

---

## 5. Trap, Interrupt, and Debug Behavior

### 5.1 Interrupt Pending and Enable

The module must maintain and output the machine interrupt-enable and interrupt-pending state.

It must also output a global interrupt-enable qualifier that is:

- False while in debug mode.
- False while single-stepping and interrupts-during-single-step are disabled.
- True for machine mode only when machine interrupts are enabled.
- True for S/U mode subject to the separately provided supervisor interrupt-enable and delegation information.

### 5.2 Trap Entry

When a synchronous exception or interrupt is accepted while not in debug mode, the module must:

- Determine whether the trap is delegated to S-mode or taken in M-mode.
- A trap is delegated if it was caused by an interrupt and the corresponding `mideleg` bit is set, or by a synchronous exception and the corresponding `medeleg` bit is set.
- A trap never transitions from a more-privileged mode to a less-privileged mode. If the hart is already in M-mode, the trap remains in M-mode.

For a trap taken in S-mode:

- Disable supervisor interrupts.
- Save the previous supervisor interrupt-enable state.
- Save the previous privilege level.
- Write the cause, exception PC, and trap value to the supervisor trap CSRs.
- Set privilege level to S-mode.

For a trap taken in M-mode:

- Disable machine interrupts.
- Save the previous machine interrupt-enable state.
- Save the previous privilege level.
- Write the cause, exception PC, and trap value to the machine trap CSRs.
- Set privilege level to M-mode.

Trap value behavior must follow the configured policy: for certain exceptions, the trap value is zero; for others, it carries the faulting address or exception-specific information.

The module must output the correct trap-vector base for the selected target privilege:

- M-mode traps use the machine trap-vector base.
- S-mode traps use the supervisor trap-vector base.
- Debug mode uses the debug trap-vector base.

For interrupts taken in vectored mode, the vector base must be offset by four times the interrupt cause number.

Trap entry itself must not request a pipeline flush.

### 5.3 Trap Return

The module must support `MRET`, `SRET`, and `DRET`.

- `MRET`:
  - Selects the machine exception PC as the return PC.
  - Restores machine interrupt-enable from the saved machine previous interrupt-enable.
  - Restores the previous machine privilege level.
  - Sets the saved machine privilege field to U-mode.
  - Sets the saved machine interrupt-enable field to 1.
- `SRET`:
  - Selects the supervisor exception PC as the return PC.
  - Restores supervisor interrupt-enable from the saved supervisor previous interrupt-enable.
  - Restores the previous supervisor privilege level.
  - Clears the saved supervisor privilege field.
  - Sets the saved supervisor interrupt-enable field to 1.
- `DRET`:
  - Selects the debug PC as the return PC.
  - Restores the privilege level recorded in the debug control/status register.
  - Leaves debug mode.

### 5.4 Debug Mode Entry

The module must enter debug mode on the following events:

- An enabled `ebreak` instruction, according to the per-privilege-mode ebreak enable bits.
- A debug-request exception.
- Completion of a single instruction while single-step is enabled.

When debug mode is entered:

- The previous privilege level must be recorded.
- The debug PC must be set to the appropriate resume address.
- The debug cause must be recorded.
- A request must be issued to redirect fetch to the debug trap-vector base.

While in debug mode:

- The effective privilege level is machine mode.
- Ordinary traps do not update the machine/supervisor trap CSRs.
- An `ebreak` while already in debug mode must redirect fetch to the debug vector.
- Single-step behavior is controlled by the debug control/status register.

### 5.5 Wait for Interrupt

When the `WFI` operation is accepted and the hart is not in debug mode and no exception is present, the module must enter the WFI halt state.

It must remain halted until one of the following occurs:

- Any enabled interrupt is pending.
- A debug request is asserted.
- The supervisor external interrupt line is asserted.

In the WFI halt state, the module must assert the halt request to the core.

---

## 6. Other Functional Outputs

The module must provide the following control information to the rest of the core:

- Current effective privilege level.
- Debug-mode active indication.
- Single-step active indication.
- Floating-point extension state, dynamic rounding mode, and precision control.
- Vector extension state.
- Machine and supervisor interrupt enable/pending/delegation information.
- Global interrupt-enable qualifier.
- Address-translation enable for instruction fetch.
- Address-translation enable for loads and stores.
- Effective privilege level for loads and stores, including MPRV behavior.
- `SUM` and `MXR` status bits.
- Page-table root PPN and ASID from `satp`.
- `TVM`, `TW`, and `TSR` status bits.
- Configured PMP entries to the PMP check logic.
- Machine counter-inhibit value to the performance-counter unit.
- Cache-enable and accelerator-consistency outputs.
- Pipeline flush request when a side-effect CSR write occurs.
- Halt request for WFI.
- Debug PC redirect request.
- Trap-vector base and trap-return PC.

---

## 7. Summary of Side-Effect Rules

The module must request a pipeline flush on writes that can change execution behavior across the pipeline, including writes to:

- Floating-point accrued-exception flags.
- Floating-point rounding mode.
- Combined floating-point control/status.
- Custom floating-point precision control.
- Supervisor status.
- Supervisor address translation and protection.
- Machine status.

Other CSR writes, trap entry, and trap return do not request this flush.

All CSR updates must be suppressed when the access is illegal, and no architectural state may change.

# Design Specification: RISC-V Common Definitions Package

## 1. Purpose

This unit is a SystemVerilog package that provides a common set of RISC-V definitions for the CVA6 core. It is not a hardware block with state or ports. Instead, it shall supply constants, types, enums, structures, and instruction-generation functions that can be imported by other RTL and verification units.

The package shall be configuration-consistent: all definitions that depend on the configured base integer register width shall automatically select the correct values for a 32-bit or 64-bit RISC-V implementation.

---

## 2. Configuration-Dependent Behavior

### 2.1 Integer and Address Widths

When the configured integer register width is 32 bits:

- The integer register type shall be 32 bits wide.
- The virtual address width shall be 32 bits.
- The physical address width shall be 34 bits.
- The address-translation mode field width shall be 1 bit.
- The address-space identifier field width shall be 9 bits.
- The physical page number field width shall be 22 bits.
- The default virtual-memory scheme shall be Sv32.
- The effective virtual-memory scheme size shall be 32 bits.

When the configured integer register width is 64 bits:

- The integer register type shall be 64 bits wide.
- The virtual address width shall be 64 bits.
- The physical address width shall be 56 bits.
- The address-translation mode field width shall be 4 bits.
- The address-space identifier field width shall be 16 bits.
- The physical page number field width shall be 44 bits.
- The default virtual-memory scheme shall be Sv39.
- The effective virtual-memory scheme size shall be 39 bits.

The package shall also provide a boolean indication of whether the configuration is RV32 or RV64, and a byte-alignment constant derived from the integer register width.

### 2.2 Virtual-Memory Mode Encodings

The package shall define the virtual-memory mode encodings required by the RISC-V privileged specification:

- Bare mode.
- Sv32.
- Sv39.
- Sv48.
- Sv57.
- Sv64.

These encodings shall be usable to distinguish bare translation from page-based 32-bit, 39-bit, 48-bit, 57-bit, and 64-bit virtual-memory schemes.

---

## 3. Privilege and Status Definitions

### 3.1 Privilege Levels

The package shall define privilege-level encodings for:

- User mode.
- Supervisor mode.
- Machine mode.

The encoding shall match the RISC-V privileged specification.

### 3.2 XLEN Encoding

The package shall define an enumeration for base integer register widths:

- 32-bit.
- 64-bit.
- 128-bit.

### 3.3 Extension State

The package shall define an extension-state type with the four RISC-V states:

- Off.
- Initial.
- Clean.
- Dirty.

### 3.4 Machine and Supervisor Status Layouts

The package shall define packed structures for the machine status and supervisor status registers. These structures shall represent the standard RISC-V status fields, including:

- Global interrupt enables for user, supervisor, and machine modes.
- Previous interrupt enables.
- Previous privilege levels.
- Make-executable-readable and supervisor-user-memory access fields.
- Modify-privilege field.
- Trap SRET, timeout-wait, and trap-virtual-memory fields.
- Floating-point state, vector state, and extension state.
- State-dirty read-only indication.
- Reserved fields that preserve written values and ignore reads.

The supervisor status structure shall be the supervisor-visible subset of the machine status structure.

### 3.5 Supervisor Address Translation and Protection

The package shall define a structure for the `satp` register, containing:

- The address-translation mode.
- The address-space identifier.
- The physical page number of the root page table.

The field widths of this structure shall depend on the configured integer register width as described in Section 2.1.

---

## 4. Instruction Formats and Opcode Definitions

### 4.1 Instruction Format Structures

The package shall define packed structures for the standard RISC-V instruction formats:

- R-type.
- R4-type.
- R-type for floating-point operations.
- Vector floating-point R-type.
- I-type.
- S-type.
- U-type.
- Atomic-type.

These structures shall place each instruction field in its architectural bit position.

The package shall also define a union type that can view a 32-bit instruction word as any of the above formats. This allows instruction decoding to interpret fields such as opcode, source registers, destination register, function codes, and immediate bits from a single instruction word.

### 4.2 Base Opcode Constants

The package shall define the 7-bit opcode constants for the RV32/RV64 base and extension instruction spaces, including:

- Load and load-floating-point.
- Store and store-floating-point.
- OP-IMM and OP.
- OP-IMM-32 and OP-32.
- LUI and AUIPC.
- Branch.
- JAL and JALR.
- System.
- AMO.
- Misc-memory.
- Custom opcode spaces.
- Floating-point fused multiply-add operations.
- Floating-point operation.
- Vector operation.
- Reserved opcode spaces.

### 4.3 Compressed Opcode Constants

The package shall define the compressed instruction quadrant values and the function-three selectors for RV32C/RV64C compressed instructions, including:

- Quadrant 0: stack-relative loads/stores, loads/stores, and compressed Zcb subset.
- Quadrant 1: integer/control-flow operations such as addi, jal, li, lui, addi16sp, misc-ALU, jump, conditional branches.
- Quadrant 2: stack-relative loads/stores, shifts, jalr/mv/add, and floating-point loads/stores.

---

## 5. Virtual Memory Page-Table Entry Definitions

The package shall define page-table entry structures for 32-bit and 64-bit virtual-memory systems.

Each page-table entry shall include:

- Valid bit.
- Read, write, and execute permission bits.
- User-mode access bit.
- Global bit.
- Accessed bit.
- Dirty bit.
- Reserved-for-software field.
- Physical page number.

The physical page number width shall be:

- 22 bits for the 32-bit page-table entry format.
- 44 bits for the 64-bit page-table entry format.

The remaining layout shall match the RISC-V privileged specification for Sv32 and Sv39 page-table entries.

---

## 6. Exception and Interrupt Definitions

### 6.1 Exception Cause Codes

The package shall define synchronous exception cause codes for:

- Instruction address misaligned.
- Instruction access fault.
- Illegal instruction.
- Breakpoint.
- Load address misaligned.
- Load access fault.
- Store/AMO address misaligned.
- Store/AMO access fault.
- Environment call from user mode.
- Environment call from supervisor mode.
- Environment call from machine mode.
- Instruction page fault.
- Load page fault.
- Store/AMO page fault.
- Debug request.

These cause codes shall match the exception code values described in the RISC-V privileged specification.

### 6.2 Interrupt Numbers and Masks

The package shall define interrupt numbers for:

- Supervisor software interrupt.
- Machine software interrupt.
- Supervisor timer interrupt.
- Machine timer interrupt.
- Supervisor external interrupt.
- Machine external interrupt.

It shall also define:

- Pending-bit masks for the machine interrupt-pending register.
- Combined interrupt cause values with the interrupt bit set.

---

## 7. CSR Address and Access Definitions

### 7.1 CSR Address Enumeration

The package shall define named constants for the control and status register addresses used by the core, including:

- Floating-point CSRs: accrued exceptions, dynamic rounding mode, floating-point control/status, and floating-point custom control.
- Vector CSRs.
- Supervisor CSRs: status, interrupt enable, trap vector, counter enable, scratch, exception program counter, cause, trap value, interrupt pending, and address translation/protection.
- Machine CSRs: status, ISA, exception/interrupt delegation, interrupt enable, trap vector, counter enable, counter inhibit, scratch, exception program counter, cause, trap value, interrupt pending, PMP configuration and address registers, vendor/architecture/implementation/hart ID registers, and machine configuration pointer.
- Performance-monitoring CSRs: cycle and instruction-retired counters, event selectors, and their upper-half shadows.
- User-mode read-only counter shadows.
- Cache-control CSRs.
- Trigger/debug CSRs: trigger select, trigger data, trigger info, debug control/status, debug PC, and debug scratch registers.

### 7.2 CSR Access Opcodes

The package shall define the CSR instruction function codes:

- CSRRW.
- CSRRS.
- CSRRC.
- CSRRWI.
- CSRRSI.
- CSRRCI.

### 7.3 Decoded CSR Address

The package shall define a decoded representation of a 12-bit CSR address. The decoded form shall expose:

- Read/write access behavior.
- Required privilege level.
- Low address bits.

This shall allow a CSR access to be checked for privilege and read/write eligibility.

### 7.4 Status Register Field Masks

The package shall define masks for the fields of `mstatus` and `sstatus`, including:

- Global and previous interrupt enables.
- Previous privilege fields.
- Floating-point and extension state fields.
- SUM, MXR, MPRV, TVM, TW, and TSR fields.
- UXL and SXL field positions.
- State-dirty bit position.

The state-dirty mask shall select bit 31 for a 32-bit configuration and bit 63 for a 64-bit configuration.

---

## 8. Floating-Point Control/Status Register Layout

The package shall define a structure for the floating-point control and status register. The layout shall include:

- Accrued exception flags: invalid operation, divide-by-zero, overflow, underflow, and inexact.
- Dynamic rounding mode.
- Floating-point precision control field.
- Reserved upper bits.

This structure shall represent the programmer-visible floating-point CSR fields.

---

## 9. Physical Memory Protection Definitions

### 9.1 Address Modes

The package shall define PMP address-mode encodings:

- Off.
- Top-of-range.
- Naturally aligned 4-byte.
- Naturally aligned power-of-two.

### 9.2 PMP Configuration Structure

The package shall define a packed configuration structure for one PMP entry containing:

- Lock bit.
- Address mode.
- Execute permission.
- Write permission.
- Read permission.
- Reserved bits.

This structure shall match the architectural layout of a PMP configuration byte.

---

## 10. Debug Control/Status Layout

The package shall define a packed structure for the debug control and status register. The structure shall include:

- Debug version.
- `ebreak` behavior in machine, supervisor, and user modes.
- Single-step interrupt enable.
- Stop-count and stop-time controls.
- Debug-entry cause.
- Modify-privilege enable.
- Non-maskable interrupt pending.
- Single-step enable.
- Privilege level at debug entry.

---

## 11. Instruction-Generation Functions

The package shall provide functions that return complete 32-bit instruction words for common instructions. These functions shall place immediate fields, register fields, function codes, and opcodes in the architectural positions required by the base RISC-V ISA.

The functions shall support generation of:

- `jal`: jump-and-link with a 21-bit immediate offset.
- `jalr`: jump-and-link-register with a 12-bit offset.
- `andi`: AND-immediate.
- `slli`: shift-left-logical-immediate.
- `srli`: shift-right-logical-immediate.
- `load`: integer load with a size select and 12-bit offset.
- `auipc`: add-upper-immediate-to-PC.
- `store`: integer store with a size select and 12-bit offset.
- `float_load`: floating-point load.
- `float_store`: floating-point store.
- `csrw`: CSR write using CSRRW with the destination register set to `x0`.
- `csrr`: CSR read using CSRRS with the source register set to `x0`.
- `branch`: branch with a 12-bit offset and function-three select.

The package shall also provide fixed instruction-word generators for:

- `ebreak`.
- `wfi`.
- `nop`.
- A reserved/illegal instruction word.

All generated instruction words shall be 32 bits wide and shall be suitable for use as executable instruction encodings.

---

## 12. Simulation Trace Support

The package shall provide simulation-only definitions compatible with a RISC-V architectural commit-log trace.

The trace formatting function shall:

- Accept a privilege level, program counter, instruction word, destination register number, result value, and a flag indicating whether the destination is a floating-point register.
- Format a line containing the privilege level, program counter, and instruction word.
- Display a 16-bit instruction word when the instruction is compressed and a 32-bit word otherwise.
- Include the destination register and result value when a destination register is written.
- Omit the destination register and result when no integer destination register is written, i.e. when the destination is the `x0` register and the destination is not a floating-point register.

The package shall also define a trace record type suitable for holding a single commit-log event, including privilege, PC, floating-point flag, destination register, result data, instruction word, and exception flag.

These simulation-only definitions shall not affect synthesized hardware behavior.

---

## 13. Summary of Observable Behavior

The observable behavior of this package is limited to the definitions and functions it exports. Any unit importing this package shall receive:

- Consistent configuration-dependent RISC-V widths and enums.
- Instruction format and opcode definitions.
- Virtual-memory and page-table definitions.
- Exception, interrupt, and CSR address constants.
- Status-register, floating-point CSR, PMP, and debug register layouts.
- Instruction-generation functions returning valid RISC-V instruction encodings.
- Simulation trace support for commit-log generation.

The package shall not contain stateful behavior, timing, or module-to-module communication.
